newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO-Russia set new round of talks on enlargement.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia set new round of talks on enlargement.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana will meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Brussels on February 23 for a second round of talks aimed at trying to clinch a deal over the alliance's planned enlargement.

Alliance diplomats say the talks will centre on a permanent consultative mechanism between Moscow and the alliance and other inducements offered by the West to try and meet Russian objections to NATO's expansion into former communist Europe.

A first round of talks, held at a guest house outside Moscow on January 20, made little progress, but since then the NATO allies have stepped up diplomatic efforts to entice Russia into serious negotiations.
Last week, U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott -- the U.S. administration's point man on relations with Russia -- met Primakov and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov.

A package of measures drawn up by Talbott hints at concessions on outstanding arms control issues, particularly cuts in the U.S.'s submarine-based nuclear missile arsenal, more financial aid, and Russian membership of the Group of Seven (G-7).

This weekend French President Jacques Chirac flies to Moscow as the first Western leader to have a face-to-face meeting with President Boris Yeltsin since the Russian leader's recovery from pneumonia.
Solana visited Chirac, a keen advocate of NATO enlargement and good relations with Russia, in Paris earlier this week to brief him on the state of talks.

"The president believes that NATO enlargement must go ahead while taking account of Russia's concerns. It is important not to create new divisions in Europe," presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.
France sympathises with Russia's arguement that any document between the two sides should be legally binding.
The U.S. envisages a document, signed by the heads of government, which would be politically binding.
"A formal treaty would be cumbersome and slow," said one U.S. diplomatic source.

NATO is keen to have a deal with Russia ready for July when a summit in Madrid will name the alliance's first new members for over two decades. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic lead the field with Romania and Slovenia close behind.

NATO diplomats hailed Primakov's confirmation of a new meeting as further evidence Solana had been accepted by Moscow as the West's main negotiator on a new pact or charter covering all relations between the old Cold War enemies.
"It is good news for Solana, he seems to have succeeded in convincing the Russians he is the man to deal with," said one alliance diplomat.
Solana, who sees the negotiations with Russia as the main challenge of his tenure of the secretary-generalship, sought again on Thursday to soothe Russian anxieties about enlargement.

Speaking to the Council of Europe in Strasbourg, he acknowledged time would be needed to convince Moscow the alliance's growth was not intended to harm Russian interests, but spread stability in Europe.

"A European security architecture worth its name must be one that gives the largest European state, Russia, its rightful place and enables Russia to make its full contribution," Solana told the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly.
"The opening of NATO is therefore in no sense aimed at isolating or marginalising Russia," Solana said, adding:
